about: The vessel tree, as centrelines with radii. Positions are in the same body-local space as src/data/organs.json, so a renal artery ends where the kidney is. Radii are luminal radii in metres at the vessel's origin, tapering to the value at its end; the model is a tapered tube, which is what a real vessel is. Nothing here affects the simulation — the haemodynamics are lumped-compartment and live in src/sim/systems/cardio.ts. This file exists so the circulation can be SEEN, and it is a drawing, not a model.

GRAYS41.label: Standring S (ed). Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 41st ed. Elsevier, 2016.

WOLTERS2015.label: Wolters BJBM, et al. A mathematical model for abdominal aortic aneurysm; and the normal aortic diameters it reports. (Normal infrarenal aortic diameter 1.0-1.5 cm.)

ENGINEERING.label: Engineering default chosen so the drawing reads correctly at the scale this body is rendered at. Not an anatomical measurement; see docs/MODEL_LIMITATIONS.md.

radiusNote: Radii are halved diameters from Gray's where Gray's gives a diameter, and are marked 'assumed' where the vessel is drawn for continuity rather than measured. A vessel drawn at an invented radius would be a number this project forbids, so every entry declares which it is.

segments.label: Ascending aorta
segments.note: Adult ascending aortic diameter about 2.9 cm at the sinotubular junction. Starts at the heart's own centre so the tree is continuous with the chamber model.

segments.label: Aortic arch
segments.note: Arches posteriorly and to the left over the left main bronchus, then descends. The posterior sweep is what makes the vascular view read as three-dimensional rather than as a flat diagram.

segments.label: Descending thoracic aorta
segments.note: Descends on the left of the vertebral bodies and moves toward the midline as it goes. Diameter about 2.4 cm falling to 2.1.

segments.label: Abdominal aorta
segments.note: Normal infrarenal diameter 1.0-1.5 cm, so a radius near 0.6 cm at the bifurcation. The taper from thoracic to infrarenal is real and substantial.

segments.label: Left common carotid
segments.note: Common carotid diameter about 6.3 mm. Runs to the brain, which is why a carotid occlusion is a neurological event and not a vascular one.

segments.label: Right common carotid
segments.note: Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk rather than directly from the arch, which is the asymmetry drawn here.

segments.label: Left subclavian
segments.note: Subclavian diameter about 9 mm. The last branch of the arch.

segments.label: Right subclavian
segments.note: Via the brachiocephalic trunk.

segments.label: Pulmonary trunk
segments.note: Diameter about 2.7 cm. Carries DEOXYGENATED blood, which is the single most counter-intuitive fact in the circulation and the reason this tree is coloured by saturation rather than by whether it is an artery.

segments.label: Left pulmonary artery
segments.note: Ends at the left lung's centre, as positioned in organs.json.

segments.label: Right pulmonary artery
segments.note: Longer than the left because the pulmonary trunk sits left of midline.

segments.label: Left pulmonary veins
segments.note: Carries OXYGENATED blood back to the left atrium. Drawn as one trunk per side rather than the real two, which is a simplification stated in docs/VASCULAR.md.

segments.label: Right pulmonary veins
segments.note: As for the left.

segments.label: Coeliac trunk
segments.note: Short and wide, about 8 mm, supplying stomach, liver and spleen. Ends between the stomach and spleen as positioned.

segments.label: Hepatic artery
segments.note: One of the liver's two blood supplies, and the minor one: about a quarter of hepatic flow. The portal vein carries the rest.

segments.label: Superior mesenteric artery
segments.note: Diameter about 7 mm, supplying the small intestine. Its flow rises substantially after a meal, which is the splanchnic steal that makes exercise after eating uncomfortable.

segments.label: Left renal artery
segments.note: Diameter about 5.5 mm. Carries roughly a fifth of cardiac output to an organ that is 0.4% of body mass, which is why renal perfusion is so sensitive to pressure.

segments.label: Right renal artery
segments.note: Longer than the left because the aorta lies left of midline.

segments.label: Left common iliac
segments.note: Diameter about 1.1 cm at the bifurcation.

segments.label: Right common iliac
segments.note: Mirror of the left.

segments.label: Inferior vena cava
segments.note: Widens as it ascends and receives tributaries, reaching about 2.6 cm at the diaphragm. It lies to the RIGHT of the aorta, which is the asymmetry that makes the venous and arterial trees distinguishable at a glance.

segments.label: Superior vena cava
segments.note: Diameter about 2 cm. Drains the head, neck and upper limbs into the right atrium.

segments.label: Left internal jugular
segments.note: Larger than the carotid it runs beside, as veins generally are: the same flow at a fraction of the pressure needs more area.

segments.label: Right internal jugular
segments.note: Usually the larger of the two, and more directly in line with the SVC, which is why it is the preferred side for central access.

segments.label: Portal vein
segments.note: Diameter about 1.1 cm. THE MOST IMPORTANT VESSEL IN THIS SIMULATION: it carries everything absorbed from the gut to the liver before the body sees it, which is first-pass metabolism, which is why an oral dose and an intravenous dose of the same drug are different drugs.

segments.label: Hepatic veins
segments.note: Drains the liver into the IVC just below the diaphragm. Everything that survived the first pass leaves by this route.

segments.label: Left renal vein
segments.note: Crosses the midline anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC, which is why it is notably longer than the right.

segments.label: Right renal vein
segments.note: Short, because the IVC lies on the right.

segments.label: Left common iliac vein
segments.note: Crosses to the right to join the IVC.

segments.label: Right common iliac vein
segments.note: Shorter and more direct than the left.

segments.label: Left coronary artery
segments.note: Left main diameter about 4.5 mm. Arises from the aortic root and fills in DIASTOLE, not systole, because in systole the myocardium it supplies is squeezing it shut. That is the reason coronary perfusion pressure is a diastolic quantity in systems/procedures.ts.

segments.label: Right coronary artery
segments.note: Diameter about 3.9 mm. Supplies the sinoatrial node in most people, which is why a right coronary occlusion causes bradycardia.

segments.label: Left anterior descending
segments.note: Geometry drawn for continuity down the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex; the LAD is 'the widow-maker' because it feeds most of the left ventricle. Left-main radius near 2 mm tapers to under 1 mm here per Gray's; the centreline itself is an engineering approximation, not a measurement.

segments.label: Left circumflex artery
segments.note: Curls left in the atrioventricular groove toward the posterior heart. Radius basis Gray's (circumflex ~1.5 mm); the path is drawn so a small coronary vessel is visible, so this is an engineering geometry rather than a segmentation.

segments.label: Right marginal branch
segments.note: Runs down the acute margin of the right ventricle. A small vessel added so the coronary supply reads as a branching tree rather than two stubs; geometry is an engineering default, radius scale from Gray's.

segments.label: Basilar artery
segments.note: Formed by the vertebral arteries and ascending the front of the brainstem to the circle of Willis. Basilar diameter about 3 mm per Gray's; the vertebral supply is elided and the path is an engineering approximation so the posterior cerebral circulation is at least suggested.

segments.label: Left middle cerebral artery
segments.note: From the internal carotid termination into the Sylvian fissure and out over the hemisphere. Drawn as a single sweep standing in for the circle of Willis and the cerebral tree; MCA radius near 1.5 mm from Gray's, geometry an engineering default.

segments.label: Right middle cerebral artery
segments.note: Mirror of the left. A carotid supplies the brain on its own side, which is why a carotid embolus is a one-sided stroke; this is a drawn approximation, not a segmentation.

segments.label: Anterior cerebral arteries
segments.note: The midline pair sweeping up between the hemispheres over the corpus callosum. Drawn as one midline vessel to complete the circle-of-Willis suggestion; an engineering geometry with a Gray's-scale radius.

segments.label: Splenic artery
segments.note: The most tortuous artery in the body in life; drawn here as a smooth curve from the coeliac trunk to the spleen. Splenic radius about 2 mm per Gray's; the tortuous course is not reproduced, so the geometry is an engineering approximation.

segments.label: Left gastric artery
segments.note: The smallest branch of the coeliac trunk, running to the lesser curve of the stomach. Added so the coeliac trifurcation reads as three vessels; geometry an engineering default, radius from Gray's.

segments.label: Inferior mesenteric artery
segments.note: Supplies the descending and sigmoid colon from low on the aorta. IMA diameter about 3 mm per Gray's; the watershed with the SMA at the splenic flexure is the reason ischaemic colitis strikes there. Path is an engineering approximation.

segments.label: Jejunal arteries
segments.note: One branch of the SMA fan into the small-bowel mesentery, drawn to make the mesenteric supply read as a tree reaching the gut rather than stopping at the aorta. Engineering geometry; small-artery radius scale from Gray's.

segments.label: Ileal arteries
segments.note: A second SMA branch to the ileum on the right of the mesenteric fan. Added for visible small vessels within the abdomen; an engineering-default path, radius from Gray's.

segments.label: Left brachial artery
segments.note: Continues the axillary artery down the medial arm; it is the vessel a blood-pressure cuff occludes. Brachial radius about 2 mm per Gray's; the limb is not modelled in organs.json, so its path is an engineering default drawn to give the arterial tree limbs.

segments.label: Right brachial artery
segments.note: Mirror of the left brachial. An engineering geometry, since the limbs are drawn for the vasculature view rather than positioned from organs.json.

segments.label: Left femoral artery
segments.note: The continuation of the external iliac into the thigh; the common femoral is the standard arterial-access site. Femoral radius about 4 mm per Gray's; the leg is not in organs.json so this centreline is an engineering approximation.

segments.label: Right femoral artery
segments.note: Mirror of the left femoral. Engineering geometry drawn so the arterial tree extends into both legs.

segments.label: Left popliteal artery
segments.note: Behind the knee, continuing the femoral before it trifurcates in the calf. Added so the leg supply tapers realistically; an engineering path, radius scale from Gray's.

segments.label: Right popliteal artery
segments.note: Mirror of the left. Engineering geometry for the distal leg.

segments.label: Splenic vein
segments.note: Drains the spleen and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein; it is portal, not systemic, so what it carries goes to the liver first. Radius from Gray's (~3 mm); path is an engineering approximation converging on the portal confluence.

segments.label: Superior mesenteric vein
segments.note: Carries everything absorbed from the small bowel up to the portal confluence — the first leg of first-pass metabolism. Radius from Gray's (~6 mm at the confluence); geometry an engineering default authored gut-to-liver so its particles flow the right way.

segments.label: Left brachial vein
segments.note: Paired deep vein of the arm, authored periphery-to-heart so it flows opposite its companion artery. Veins run wider than their arteries at the same flow; radius scale from Gray's, path an engineering default for the limb.

segments.label: Right brachial vein
segments.note: Mirror of the left brachial vein. Engineering geometry, flow authored toward the subclavian.

segments.label: Left femoral vein
segments.note: The deep vein returning the leg, and the commonest source of a deep-vein thrombosis. Authored leg-to-pelvis so it flows into the iliac vein; radius from Gray's, path an engineering approximation.

segments.label: Right femoral vein
segments.note: Mirror of the left femoral vein. Engineering geometry, flow authored toward the iliac vein.

segments.label: Left lobar pulmonary artery
segments.note: A lobar division of the left pulmonary artery carrying deoxygenated blood deeper into the lung. Drawn so the pulmonary tree branches into the lung rather than ending at its hilum; radius scale from Gray's, path an engineering default. It stays coloured dark because it is a pulmonary ARTERY.

segments.label: Right lobar pulmonary artery
segments.note: Lobar division on the right, where there are three lobes to the left's two. Engineering geometry; carries the body's most deoxygenated blood, so it is drawn dark.

segments.label: Left pulmonary vein tributary
segments.note: A tributary gathering freshly oxygenated blood from the lung back toward the pulmonary vein trunk — authored lung-to-heart so it flows correctly. It is the brightest blood in the body; radius scale from Gray's, path an engineering approximation.

segments.label: Right pulmonary vein tributary
segments.note: Tributary on the right, flowing lung-to-heart. Engineering geometry; drawn bright because a pulmonary VEIN carries oxygenated blood, the counter-intuitive case this whole tree is coloured to show.
